analysis.one_liner: Caps rent-to-Store fees at state credit-sale limits and extends federal consumer credit protections to rent-to-own contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with bipartisan sponsorship, never received a vote in the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: Rent-to-own stores let customers take home furniture, appliances, and electronics with weekly payments until they own the item. The bill would have capped the fees and finance charges rent-to-own dealers can charge at the levels state law allows for ordinary installment sales, required price tags showing the cash price, the annual percentage rate, and the total cost to own, extended federal lending and debt-collection protections to these contracts, and let customers sue for violations. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Rent-to-own customers, who are disproportionately low-income and live in minority neighborhoods, would gain clear upfront disclosure of what an item really costs to buy over time, limits on fees and charges comparable to what installment buyers get, protection from abusive collection tactics like threats of criminal prosecution, and the right to sue violators.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would bar rent-to-own sellers from charging interest, finance charges, or fees above what state law allows for a credit or installment sale of the same item [S2].

Sellers would have to post on each item the cash price, the annual percentage rate, each periodic payment, the total number of payments to acquire ownership, and whether the item is new or used, and provide the same information in writing at signing [S2].

Four federal consumer laws would apply to rent-to-own contracts: the Truth in Lending Act, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, and the Fair Credit Reporting Act [S2].

Sellers could not threaten criminal prosecution, use threats or coercion to collect payments, or unreasonably disclose a customer's debts to third parties; the FTC could enforce the rules and violators would face civil liability of up to $5,000 per violation plus damages and attorney fees [S2].

The bill's own findings state that rent-to-own dealers often fail to disclose key contract terms, engage in unfair debt collection, charge excessive fees and rates, and target low-income and minority neighborhoods [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Rent-to-own dealers would bear the cost: their fees and finance charges would be capped at installment-sale levels, they would face new disclosure and paperwork requirements, and they would be exposed to lawsuits and FTC enforcement for violations.

drawbacks.text: Caps keyed to state installment-sale law could squeeze dealers' revenue, and some cost could be passed to customers through higher base rents or fewer stores, particularly in low-margin neighborhoods; the bill text anticipates this pressure by allowing a termination fee of up to 5% of the cash price and reasonable item-recovery fees [S3].

Rent-to-own contracts are cancellable leases, not loans, and the industry's long-standing argument is that customers pay for the flexibility to walk away at any time; folding these contracts into credit-sale law would take away pricing flexibility that some customers value, even if it lowers the total cost of ownership.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For customers who complete a contract, total costs would likely fall substantially, since rent-to-own totals often far exceed the cash price of the item, and disclosure would make that visible before signing. The main trade-off is that dealers' margins would shrink and the walk-away flexibility that justifies part of the premium would be priced and regulated more like credit. On balance the bill transfers cost from low-income households to the industry, with disclosure and enforcement rights as the backbone.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in October 1993 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it; it died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum, joined by Senator Dave Durenberger and one other cosponsor, introduced the bill on October 19, 1993 [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and bills not passed by then expire [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rent-to-own dealers are better off: the fee caps, disclosure rules, and collection-practice limits never took effect, so contracts continued on the industry's own terms.

for.name: Sen. Howard M. Metzenbaum
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on October 19, 1993.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 19, 1993 and never reported it out; no hearing or markup appears in the record.

against.name: Rent-to-own store industry
against.role: Industry whose contracts the bill would regulate
against.what_they_did: Opposed efforts in this era to bring rent-to-own contracts under credit-sale pricing and disclosure rules, arguing the contracts are leases, not credit.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan at introduction — a Democratic sponsor with one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor — but it drew no committee action from either party.

industries.note: The bill would cap the fees and charges these dealers can impose at installment-sale levels, require upfront disclosure of the true total cost to own, and expose them to FTC enforcement and lawsuits. Dealers profit from the gap between the cash price of goods and the much larger total of payments, so their interest in this bill ran against their customers'.
